results.title: Cloud Pricing Goes Dynamic — The Without Surprise Blog
results.author: Timothy O’Brien
highlights:
Cloud prices are moving again, and the movement looks like a change in the pricing regime rather than a run of one-off adjustments. Between September 17 and October 1, Nebius told customers that on-demand GPU rates would rise roughly 17 to 21 percent and memory-backed capacity about 41 percent, effective October 1. 1 2 OVHcloud unbundled local storage and public IPv4 addresses from its Public Cloud instances on the same date, which moved the price of an identical configuration up 1.4 to 21.9 percent depending on size. 3 CoreWeave announced that it has continued to contract new compute capacity at higher prices, on short terms of roughly three to six months. 4 Under all three announcements sits the same pressure: memory. TrendForce’s September 30 survey projects conventional DRAM contract prices up another 10 to 15 percent in the fourth quarter, after a year of much larger increases, with server DRAM undersupplied into 2027. 5

...

Nebius notified customers on September 17 rather than issuing a press release: new on-demand rates take effect October 1. 1 The increases step up by chip generation, about 17 percent on H100 instances, 20 percent on H200, 19 percent on B200, 21 percent on the newest B300s, with AMD CPU rates up about 25 percent and memory-backed instances up roughly 41 percent, the largest single line in the notice. It was the company’s second increase in roughly three months. 2 The stock market read the notice as pricing power rather than distress: Nebius shares climbed about 10 percent that morning, and operators that had sent no note at all caught a bid alongside it. 6 The detail to notice is the memory line. Providers bundle memory into instance pricing, so it rarely appears on its own on a bill. A 41 percent increase on the memory line says the component inside every instance is repricing, not just the scarce GPUs on top.

...

1. Yahoo Finance, September 17, 2026: Nebius Group (NBIS) Raises AI Cloud Prices As Compute Demand Tests Customer Costs — customer communication rather than a public release; higher on-demand rates effective October 1, 2026; compute demand as the stated driver.

results.title: Nebius moves spare GPU hours to spot prices | Wire
results.author: Sean
highlights:
# Nebius moves spare GPU hours to spot prices from $0.79

Nebius switched its spare GPU hours from a fixed price to live spot pricing on 8 October. An H100 hour now floats between $0.79 and $4.49. Nebius gets paid more when clusters are full. The stuck step is the idle hour, and only the console shows it.

#### Sean

 09 Oct 2026 — 4 min read 

Illustrative image. Nebius H100 preemptible price band from 8 Oct 2026.

`WIRE` · `NEOCLOUDS` · `GLOBAL` · Data as at 9 Oct 2026

Nebius no longer sells its spare GPU hours at a fixed price. Since 8 October 2026, its interruptible (preemptible) GPU hours float. An H100 hour now costs anywhere from $0.79 to $4.49. Until last week it was a flat $2.15. The price moves with how full Nebius's clusters are, and it can change every 15 minutes. On the neocloud model, this is the idle-hour step: Nebius now gets paid more for spare chips when they are scarce, and less when they sit.

## What happened

Nebius, the GPU cloud that rents Nvidia chips by the hour, updated its compute price list for October. Two changes, a week apart:

8 October

Preemptible B300, B200, H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000 hours move to dynamic spot pricing

Nebius Compute pricing documentation

The band

Floor of $0.79 (H100, H200) or $0.99 (B200, B300). Ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate

Price set by capacity, cluster use, customer demand and pricing preferences

1 October

On-demand rates up 17% to 21%: H100 $3.85 to $4.50, B300 $7.85 to $9.50

This raised the spot ceiling too, since the ceiling tracks on-demand

Who can see the price

Current and past spot prices sit inside the Nebius console, not on a public page

Nebius price page, read 9 Oct 2026

...

Who gets paid. Nebius, when its clusters are full. A spare B300 hour that earned a flat $4.30 can now earn up to $9.49. The spot price also points spare chips at whoever values them most.

Who pays. Renters running batch jobs, tests and research on spare time. They used to know their price. Now they carry the price risk, on top of the risk of being kicked off.

Who waits. Buyers who want certainty. Nebius still sells multi-month cluster reservations at up to 35% off on-demand. The new spread makes that commitment look better to a renter.

Stuck step. The idle hour. The spot price now moves with how busy the clusters are, so it is a live gauge of GPU utilization. But Nebius shows it only inside its console. Outside investors can't yet see whether spare hours clear near $0.79 or near $4.49.

## Two cautions

The band is the published range, not what renters actually pay. Nebius has not said where spot prices have traded since 8 October.

Spare hours are a small slice of a GPU cloud's revenue. Most of the money comes from long contracts. This change tells you how Nebius prices its leftovers, not how much it earns.

...

Sources: Nebius, Compute pricing in Nebius AI Cloud, read 9 Oct 2026: from 1 Oct 2026 on-demand H100 $4.50 (was $3.85), H200 $5.40 (was $4.50), B200 $8.50 (was $7.15), B300 $9.50 (was $7.85); from 8 Oct 2026 preemptible pricing for B300, B200, H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000 switches to dynamic spot pricing, preemptible from $0.79 (H100, H200, RTX PRO 6000) and from $0.99 (B200, B300), previously fixed at $2.15 (H100), $2.45 (H200), $3.95 (B200), $4.30 (B300) and $0.95 (RTX PRO 6000); spot prices can change as often as every 15 minutes and the highest is one cent below the on-demand rate; Nebius price page, read 9 Oct 2026: commitment discounts of up to 35% off on-demand for multi-month cluster reservations, current spot prices shown in the Nebius console; GPU Cloud Advisors, 28 Sep 2026: 1 Oct increase of 17% to 21%. The monthly server cost examples, the ceilings as a multiple of the old price, and the spread are our arithmetic. Not investment advice. Do your own research.

results.title: Nebius lifts on-demand GPU hours up to 21% | Wire
results.author: Sean
highlights:
Nebius prices page (live 3 Oct): Oct 1 on-demand card H100 $3.85→$4.50, B300 $7.85→$9.50. A list hike is not collected cash.

#### Sean

 03 Oct 2026 — 6 min read 

`WIRE` · `NEOCLOUDS` · `GLOBAL` · Data as at 2–3 Oct 2026

Nebius’s public price page still prints two columns: the prior on-demand GPU-hour and a second column marked effective 1 October 2026. Selected Nvidia rows move 16.9% to 21.0% — H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. On the neoclouds layer, a posted card is ready list. It is not settled invoice cash until customers bill and renew at the new walk-up. Ready is not paid.

## What happened

Nebius’s prices page (live-checked 3 October 2026; FinanceFeeds confirmed both columns still visible on 2 October) posts an October 1 effective card that lifts on-demand rates on the accelerators customers are queued for. RTX PRO 6000 stays $1.80. GB200 and GB300 NVL72 racks stay contact us. Commitment discounts remain up to 35% off on-demand; spot floors print from $0.79 (H100/H200) and $0.99 (B200/B300).

...

Nebius posts Oct 1 on-demand GPU-hour card — selected Nvidia rows +16.9% to +21.0%

nebius.com/prices live-checked 3 Oct 2026; FinanceFeeds 2 Oct — both columns still printed

H100 move

$3.85 → $4.50 (+16.9%) — prior-generation Hopper still dearer to rent

8×H100 × 720h list: ~$22,176 → ~$25,920 — list math, not invoices

B300 (top of range)

$7.85 → $9.50 (+21.0%) — “up to 21%” is this row

H200 $4.50→$5.40 (+20.0%); B200 $7.15→$8.50 (+18.9%)

...

On the neoclouds layer, cash for walk-up GPU hours clears when hours are consumed and invoices clear at the rate the console bills — see Neocloud explained and Who finances GPU clusters?. A dual-column price page after the effective date is ready list talk. It is not yet paid. That gap is the whole Wire: Nebius can date the card 1 October, and still be waiting on utilization and billing when both columns sit on the same page.

...

1. Card vs bill. H100 $3.85 → $4.50 and B300 $7.85 → $9.50 are posted list moves. An 8×H100 box at 720 hours goes from about $22,176 to $25,920 on list math — before tax, storage, or a commitment discount, and not an invoice. Nebius gets paid if on-demand hours clear at the new walk-up; customers on older commitments, discounts up to 35%, or spot from $0.79/$0.99 are not paying $4.50 or $9.50.
2. GPU-hour vs megawatt. CoreWeave’s 17 September IR print is short-dated contracts (~3–6 months) at about $40 million per megawatt of annualized revenue, plus >$25 billion net new commitments early Q3 (not in the 30 June backlog) and contracted power ~ 4.2 GW as of 11 August from ~ 3.7 GW at 30 June. That is a different unit from Nebius’s GPU-hour. Do not invent an H100-equivalent hour from MW. CoreWeave gets paid if those short contracts perform; the IR does not publish a public H100 card.

...

Card effective = 1 Oct (both columns still printed 2–3 Oct). CoreWeave short-book IR = 17 Sep. Letter megawatt language = August. Settled cash = utilization + billing (and contract performance on the short MW book). Collapse them and a list hike looks like a settled invoice. It clears a billing bind toward cash. Ready is not paid.

...

The announced October 1 column is not yet the only column. FinanceFeeds’ Oct 2 check and the live page on Oct 3 still show the prior on-demand figures beside the new ones. GPU Finder was mixed (H200 new; H100/B200/B300 still showing old on one snapshot). Do not invent that every customer already pays $4.50 or $9.50.

results.title: The Compute Week Aurel Compute spent this week trying to write down what an hour of compute costs. By Thursday the question had no clean answer. | Alexandre Artus
results.author: Alexandre Artus
highlights:
The Compute Week
Aurel Compute spent this week trying to write down what an hour of compute costs. By Thursday the question had no clean answer.
Nebius raised its on-demand rates on 1 October. Its own documentation shows both grids: an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 an hour. That is still a number you can put in a spreadsheet.
The cheaper line is not. From 8 October, preemptible capacity on those GPU platforms moved to dynamic spot pricing. The documentation lists an H100 floor of $0.79, and the ceiling sits one cent under the on-demand rate, so $4.49. The price can move every fifteen minutes inside that band. A fixed $2.15 became a range of nearly six to one.
To be fair, the floor is well below the old price, and a buyer who sets a cap can do better than before. But it is no longer a figure you can put next to a rival quote, and that is what Aurel Compute has to work around.
The public reference that was meant to fix this has not arrived. CME's compute futures were slated for 5 October. Today the page still reads pending regulatory review, with no quotes and the B200 specification cells blank.
One caveat: these are advertised rates. Long reservations carry discounts, so a large buyer pays less.
Aurel Compute brokers physical capacity, Europe first: racks and hours. No derivatives, strictly neutral intermediary.
If you renewed a GPU contract this quarter, what number did you benchmark against?
Write to Aurel Compute and I will go looking.

results.title: Remember this? There are B300 cards available for $0.99/hour in the platform RIGHT NOW. | Danila Shtan

Remember this? There are B300 cards available for $0.99/hour in the platform RIGHT NOW. And capacity advisor (https://lnkd.in/e5CBpv_z) says there are plenty. :) This is always the case, when we launch new regions — the boost of available capacity drives the prices down.

Today we're introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs on Nebius. Until now, the discount on preemptible capacity has been a number we set. From October 8, the price will be calculated dynamically from available capacity and demand, for each GPU type in each region, and it will always stay below the on-demand rate. You choose how to work with it. Set a maximum price per GPU-hour and run when the price is at or below it, or follow the price and prioritize keeping your workload running. Both settings are available today, and price history will be published so you can see how the price moves before you decide. If you already run preemptible VMs, choose one of the two before October 8. Read how it works: https://lnkd.in/eKEm4aak

results.title: Together AI cuts interruptible GPU cluster compute to half price with a five-minute exit window | Beyond the News
highlights:
Together AI now offers preemptible GPU nodes at a fixed 50% discount to on-demand compute, with sub-hour billing, automatic refill and a maximum five-minute drain before reclaim. Current documentation covers Kubernetes and Slurm, but capacity and node lifetime are not guaranteed.

...

## Key details

1. September 10, 2026 announcement introduced preemptible compute in Together GPU Clusters.
2. Fixed 50% discount relative to the equivalent on-demand GPU rate, not variable spot bidding.
3. Billing is sub-hourly, metered approximately every one to two minutes.
4. Reclamation drain window is at most five minutes, with SIGTERM on Kubernetes.
5. Current documentation covers Kubernetes and Slurm public previews.
6. Requested preemptible GPU capacity is a target, not a guarantee of allocation.
7. At least one standard node is required; node classes cannot be converted in place.
8. Together attempts automatic refill after reclamation as spare capacity returns.
9. No minimum preemptible-node lifetime is guaranteed during preview.

...

Together AI introduced preemptible GPU nodes for its GPU Clusters in a September 10, 2026 public-preview announcement. The nodes use spare accelerator capacity and are billed at a fixed 50% of the equivalent on-demand rate rather than a fluctuating spot-market price. They can be added to an existing cluster alongside standard nodes, metered in one- to two-minute increments and replenished automatically toward a requested capacity target after reclamation. A reclaim notice starts a drain window of at most five minutes; workloads must checkpoint or finish before removal. The launch announcement focused on Kubernetes, while the current first-party documentation also describes public-preview support for Slurm with job requeue. The lower unit price trades away availability guarantees and predictable uninterrupted execution.

results.title: AI Neocloud vs. AWS, Azure & Google Cloud: How to Choose
results.author: Sekin Team
highlights:
Public pricing is time- and configuration-specific. Nebius says rates on its GPU pricing page are effective October 1, 2026. CoreWeave’s pricing page includes distinct on-demand and spot entries. Compare only rates that match the GPU or instance, region, duration, and billing option you would actually use, and recheck them when making a decision.

...

NVIDIA’s announcement said, “CoreWeave launches the first NVIDIA GB200 NVL72-cloud based instances to power the next era of AI reasoning.” That is a historical company announcement about a launch claim; it does not establish present-day availability, orderability, or capacity in a particular region. Check directly for the configuration and delivery window you need. See NVIDIA’s announcement.

results.title: How to Choose (and Switch) GPU Cloud Providers | Opengrid
highlights:
An on-demand H100 lists from about $1.25 an hour at developer clouds and marketplaces to $11.07 an hour at the most expensive hyperscaler.

...

So teams pick once and overpay for as long as they stay. That made sense when prices barely moved. It makes less sense now. AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement in June 2025. Then one-year H100 contract prices rose about 40% between October 2025 and March 2026. The right provider this quarter is often the wrong one next quarter. More on that in how GPU rental prices moved in 2025 and 2026.

...

Compare the quote with the whole band for that chip, not just two or three providers. Rough H100 on-demand bands as of September 2026:
